gap: No result ChatGPT got states measured idle draw. HOBOTECH measured 85 W with the Jackery Explorer 5000 Plus inverter on and no load, about 2 kWh a day or roughly 40% of its 5,040 Wh battery. pv magazine measured about 10 W for the Anker SOLIX S5000, and Zelpio measured about 18–21 W for BLUETTI's RV5 + B4810, the system inside the 5kWh RV Kit.
standout_why: Pages opened: StormWatts' 5 kWh-class solar-input comparison (cited), StormWatts' kit comparison at the same panel watts (top result), and EnergySage's best solar generators page (cited). None reports a measured figure. StormWatts says 'We have not tested these products hands-on' and gives only maker specs plus its own arithmetic. Its one measured reading is for a Jackery Explorer 2000 Plus, which is not a candidate. EnergySage says it 'did not test these models' and uses an 80–85% usable rule of thumb. None of these pages mentions idle or standby draw. Lights On Labs (cited in chat 2) would not open: WebFetch hit a certificate error and the curl fallback needed permission, so it was not checked.
decides: This confirms there is a reason to choose BLUETTI's 5kWh RV Kit, which ships now, over ChatGPT's top pick, the Jackery 5000 Plus, for multi-day outages. Zelpio measured 4,300 Wh out of the RV5 kit (84%) against HOBOTECH's 4,450 Wh from the Jackery (88%), so usable energy is close. With the AC inverter left on, though, the Jackery loses about 2,040 Wh a day against about 500 Wh for the RV5 with AC and DC on (both figures are arithmetic from the measured watts), and the RV5 kit's link price is lower. The Anker S5000 had the lowest measured idle draw (about 10 W) and the highest app-reported capacity (97%), but no panel-included Anker bundle was confirmed in this angle. The finding does not decide the pick on its own; price and shipping still do.

findings.label: Idle draw, AC inverter on, no load (HOBOTECH)
findings.source_title: The BIGGEST Jackery EVER! Explorer 5000 Plus Home Backup Solar Generator (HOBOTECH, posted 2024-11-25)
findings.note: HOBOTECH measured 515 Wh used over 6 hours with the inverter on and no load, which is 85 W. 85 W × 24 h = 2,040 Wh a day, about 40% of the 5,040 Wh rated capacity (arithmetic). DC and USB outputs at idle showed no measurable draw over 12 hours.
